694.title: Tisha B'Av: Lamentations
694.hook: read by candlelight, sitting low; the Talmud says the second Temple fell for baseless hatred (Yoma 9b)
694.howItsDone: On Tisha B'Av many Jews fast from sunset to nightfall, avoid leather shoes, sit on the floor or low stools, and hear the book of Lamentations chanted in a dim synagogue, followed by kinot, poems of mourning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fast that opens three weeks between the narrow places. Your line was walls breached. Three weeks later, the fire.

Evening, in a synagogue, on the ninth of Av. The big lights are off or turned low. In many places the curtain has been taken down from the ark. People wear sneakers or cloth shoes, because leather is set aside for the day. Nobody greets anyone. They sit on the floor or on low stools, the way mourners sit at home. Someone has a candle, someone a phone flashlight. Then a reader begins a slow, falling chant, and the first word is a cry.
screen: `THE LIGHTS GO LOW.` → `NO LEATHER, NO GREETINGS.` → `EVERYONE SITS ON THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: Eicha means how, the how you say when you can't believe what you're seeing. It's the first word of Lamentations, and Jews call the whole book by it. The old Jewish translation opens: "How doth the city sit solitary." Jerusalem, once full of people, sits alone like a widow. Of the book's five chapters, four are built on the alphabet, verse by verse, as if grief needed every letter there is. Tisha B'Av, the ninth of Av, is the day the tradition remembers both Temples falling, the first to Babylon, the second to Rome, centuries apart, mourned on one day. It's a full fast, from sunset to the next nightfall. Anyone who is ill, pregnant, nursing, or whose health would be at risk asks a doctor and a rabbi, and Jewish law puts protecting life first. Then the mourner's question: why? The Talmud, in tractate Yoma, gives a stinging answer. The first Temple fell because of idolatry, sexual sin and bloodshed. But in the second Temple's time, people studied Torah, kept the commandments and did acts of kindness. So why did it fall? Sinat chinam, baseless hatred: hatred for no reason worth the name. And baseless hatred, it says, weighs as much as those three sins together. The rabbis didn't only blame the empire with the battering rams. They looked at their own community: the feuds, the contempt, the neighbor nobody would speak to. And the book doesn't end in the dark. Its last chapter asks God to turn us back and renew our days as of old, and because the very last verse is so bitter, the congregation says that line again.
screen: `EICHA: HOW?` · `TWO TEMPLES, ONE DAY OF MOURNING.` · `NOT ONLY ROME: BASELESS HATRED.` · `SAY THE HOPEFUL LINE AGAIN.` · then, large: `BASELESS HATRED DESTROYS.`

segments.voice: If you can, sit low, on the floor or a step, and let one grudge come to mind, the kind that isn't about anything big anymore: an old slight, a neighbor you decided long ago not to like. You don't have to forgive the unforgivable or call anyone; just, for this minute, set this one down, the way you'd put a heavy bag on the floor.
Eicha. How: the first word and the Hebrew name of Lamentations, read on Tisha B'Av, sitting low. Today's word.
Your line: baseless hatred destroys. A day on the floor, asking why out loud. Until tomorrow.

695.title: Tu B'Av (Mishnah Taanit 4:8)
695.hook: six days after the saddest day comes a day of love, when young women danced in the vineyards
695.tomorrow: Year two close: the whole Torah
695.howItsDone: Tu B'Av, the fifteenth of Av, has no fixed rituals in Jewish law beyond omitting some penitential prayers; in modern Israel it is celebrated as a day of love, popular for weddings, parties and romance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Eicha, Lamentations read sitting on the floor. Your line was baseless hatred destroys. Now count six days past the floor and the candle.

There were no happier days for Israel than the fifteenth of Av and Yom Kippur. That's the claim, near the end of a Mishnah tractate about fasts, in the name of a sage called Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. Yom Kippur? The day of not eating, of standing all day in white? Happy? And the fifteenth of Av, a quiet midsummer date, sits just six days after the day Jerusalem is mourned on the floor.
screen: `NO HAPPIER DAYS THAN THESE.` → `YOM KIPPUR? HAPPY?` → `SIX DAYS AFTER THE SADDEST DAY.`

segments.voice: Tu B'Av means the fifteenth of Av: fifteen is written tet and vav, nine and six, which together sound like tu. Then the Mishnah tells what happened. On those two days the daughters of Jerusalem went out in white, and every dress was borrowed. Even the king's daughter borrowed from the high priest's daughter, and the high priest's daughter from the next family down, so no girl without a fine dress would be put to shame. Nobody could tell whose family was rich. They danced in the vineyards, calling to the young men: lift your eyes and see whom you choose. The Mishnah doesn't say why either day was so happy; the Talmud fills that in. Yom Kippur is easy: it was the day of forgiveness. For Tu B'Av it collects several reasons. On this day, it says, the tribes were first allowed to marry one another. The tribe of Benjamin, cut off after a terrible civil war in the book of Judges, was let back in. Some say the generation dying in the wilderness stopped dying. And the cutting of wood for the altar ended for the year, as the summer sun weakened. Most of the reasons are about a door opening: between tribes, back into a family, out of a long sentence. The calendar puts the two days side by side: first the floor, the candle and the cry of how; six days later, white dresses and dancing. Mourning gets its full day, and then the same month turns. In Israel today, Tu B'Av has come back as a day of love: weddings, flowers, songs on the radio.
screen: `TET AND VAV: FIFTEEN.` · `EVERY DRESS WAS BORROWED.` · `DANCING IN THE VINEYARDS.` · `A DOOR OPENS.` · then, large: `AFTER MOURNING, LOVE.`

segments.voice: Bring one person to mind, a partner, a friend, a child, a parent, someone who has stood by you in a hard stretch, and picture their face. Think of one thing about them you've never quite said out loud, something they do that makes your life lighter, and hold the person and the thing together, the way you'd hold a gift before giving it.
Tu B'Av. The fifteenth of Av: borrowed white dresses, dancing in the vineyards, and a day of love six days after mourning. Today's word.
Your line: after mourning, love. Six days from the floor to the vineyards. Day six hundred ninety-five, done.

696.title: Year two close: the whole Torah
696.hook: the whole Torah, the whole prayer book, the whole year, now known from the inside
696.carry: the torah, the prayer, the year
696.howItsDone: When the reading of each of the five books of the Torah is completed in the synagogue, the congregation, often standing, calls out "chazak, chazak, venitchazek" (be strong, be strong, and let us be strengthened), and the reader repeats it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tu B'Av, white dresses in the vineyards. Your line was after mourning, love. Today, the last day of year two.

Five times a year, something special happens in synagogue. The reader reaches the last verse of one of the Torah's five books. In some congregations everyone rises, and the whole room calls out three words: chazak, chazak, venitchazek. Be strong, be strong, and let us be strengthened. Not well done. Be strong. This year's lessons reached that shout four times: at the end of Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy. Today it comes once more, at the end of the whole year.
screen: `THE LAST VERSE OF A BOOK.` → `CHAZAK, CHAZAK, VENITCHAZEK.` → `FOUR BOOKS THIS YEAR.`

segments.voice: Year two began in the middle of the plagues and walked the people out of Egypt, through the sea, to Sinai, and into a tent of meeting built from everyone's gifts. Then Leviticus, the book of holiness, with its offerings and its sudden line, in the old Jewish translation: "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." Then Numbers: forty years of wilderness, complaints, manna and a donkey that talked. Then Deuteronomy, Moses' long goodbye, ending on Mount Nebo with a land he could see and not enter, and a grave no one knows. On Simchat Torah the scroll rolled straight back to the beginning. Then the prayer book, in order: thanking God on waking for the rooster's sense to tell day from night; the Shema, a hand over the eyes; the Amidah, feet together, three steps in; Shabbat, and the quiet personal prayers at the end. Then the year: the Days of Awe, the sukkah, winter's lights, Purim's noise, the Passover table, forty-nine days of counting, Sinai as a wedding, Ruth choosing to stay, and this summer's walls, floor and vineyards. Three circles, each one turning. The Torah is read through every year and begins again the moment it ends. The prayers come back three times a day. The year comes back every year. None is ever finished; that's the point. So the words at the end of a book don't say you made it. They say be strong, and the plural is the key: let us be strengthened, together. A people that keeps the same scroll, prayers and days holds each other up by doing it.
screen: `EXODUS TO DEUTERONOMY.` · `THE PRAYER BOOK, PAGE BY PAGE.` · `THE YEAR, FEAST AND FAST.` · `THREE CIRCLES, NEVER FINISHED.` · then, large: `THE TORAH, THE PRAYER, THE YEAR.`

segments.voice: Let a few of this year's blessings pass by: my God, the soul you placed in me is pure; the one thanking God for strength to the weary; blessed is the one who spoke, and the world came to be. If you pray, say one slowly, in Hebrew or English; if not, say quietly the one line from this year that stayed with you.
Chazak. Be strong: the shout at the end of each book of the Torah, and the word that closes the whole year, each circle beginning again.
Your line: the torah, the prayer, the year. Be strong, and let us be strengthened. Year two, complete.

697.title: Year three opens: after Moses
697.hook: the Prophets are the second part of the Tanakh; they begin the day Moses dies
697.carry: the story goes on without moses
697.howItsDone: In synagogues, each Shabbat Torah reading is followed by a haftarah, a passage from the Prophets; on Simchat Torah, as the Torah ends with Moses' death, the haftarah is commonly the opening of the book of Joshua.

segments.voice: Yesterday, chazak, a room calling out be strong as a book ends. Your line was the torah, the prayer, the year. Today, year three begins.

After the death of Moses. Those are the first words of the next book. Not a fresh start: a death, right at the top of the page. Most books start by introducing someone. This one starts by saying who is gone, and only then turns to the man left standing: Joshua son of Nun, who had served Moses. One sentence holds the old leader and the new one. The Torah has an ending. The people's story doesn't. This year, it walks on into the second part of the Bible.
screen: `AFTER THE DEATH OF MOSES.` → `WHO IS GONE, WHO IS LEFT.` → `THE STORY GOES ON.`

segments.voice: Jews call their Bible the Tanakh, a name built from the first letters of its three parts: Torah, the teaching; Nevi'im, the Prophets; Ketuvim, the Writings. Years one and two read the first part. Now, the second. Nevi'im is the plural of navi, prophet. The first surprise is what's in it. Before the prophets who speak in poetry, Nevi'im opens with books that read like history: Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings. Jewish tradition calls them the Former Prophets. So why call history prophecy? The Torah gives a clue. When Moses protests that he can't speak well enough to face Pharaoh, God answers: "Aaron thy brother shall be thy prophet." There, a navi is a spokesman, the one who carries words from one person to another. A prophet isn't mainly a fortune teller, but someone a message travels through. These books carry their message through what happens: when the people keep faith, when they don't, and what follows. The second surprise is how it starts. "Moses My servant is dead." That's God, speaking to Joshua, in the book's second verse. No long scene of grief; the Torah already gave the mourning its days. A plain sentence, then straight on: arise, cross this Jordan. The teacher of the whole Torah is gone, and the story goes on with someone new, in a harder place. That's the shape of the year ahead: a people, after Moses, working it out.
screen: `TORAH, NEVI'IM, KETUVIM.` · `IT OPENS WITH HISTORY: THE FORMER PROPHETS.` · `A NAVI CARRIES A MESSAGE.` · then, large: `MOSES MY SERVANT IS DEAD.` · then: `THE STORY GOES ON.`

segments.voice: If there's a Bible near you, Joshua's first verse is on the first page after Deuteronomy; if not, hear it in plain words: after the death of Moses, the servant of the Lord, the Lord spoke to Joshua son of Nun, who had served Moses. Keep only four words, after the death of, and let them bring to mind someone whose work you now carry on, a parent, a teacher, a friend. Stay with them a while, and with what they handed you.

698.title: Be strong (Joshua 1:1–9)
698.hook: Moses' successor is told three times, "be strong and of good courage"
698.howItsDone: The words chazak ve'ematz, be strong and of good courage, come from Joshua 1, and some say the phrase to encourage someone taking on a new task.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nevi'im, the Prophets, opening on the day Moses dies. Your line was the story goes on without moses. Today, the first words Joshua hears.

What do you say to someone on the first morning of a job far too big for them? Joshua has just stepped into Moses' place. The book's first verse calls him Moses' minister, his assistant. Now there's a river in front of him, a land of walled cities beyond it, and a whole people watching to see what happens next. God speaks. There's a promise of the land, border to border, but no battle plan, no tactics, no word about the walls. There's one phrase, said, then said again, then a third time. And before the chapter ends, someone says it back to him.
screen: `A JOB TOO BIG.` → `NO BATTLE PLAN.` → `ONE PHRASE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Listen for the repeat. First: be strong and of good courage, because you will lead this people into the land. That one is for the task. Then again, stronger: only be strong and very courageous. And the reason is a surprise. Not to fight. To keep the teaching Moses gave, turning from it neither to the right nor to the left. Then the line: "This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth, but thou shalt meditate therein day and night." The bravest thing asked of the new leader isn't a battle. It's to keep studying, to keep the words in his mouth. Then a third time, with a third reason: be strong and of good courage, don't be afraid, don't be dismayed, "for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest." The work, the teaching, and company. Now skip to the end of the chapter. Joshua gives his first orders, and the tribes whose land lies east of the Jordan answer him. Whatever you command, we'll do. Wherever you send us, we'll go. And they close with the very words he was given: only be strong and of good courage. The encouragement that came down to Joshua goes back up to him from the people. So courage here isn't a mood you wait for. It's a command. It can be spoken, repeated and handed on, from God to a leader, and from a crowd to the person in front of it.
screen: `FIRST: FOR THE TASK.` · `SECOND: FOR THE TEACHING, DAY AND NIGHT.` · `THIRD: GOD IS WITH YOU.` · then, large: `THE PEOPLE SAY IT BACK.`

699.title: Rahab (Joshua 2)
699.hook: a woman on the city wall hides the spies and asks for her family's safety; the rabbis count her among the great converts
699.howItsDone: Jews read Joshua 2 as the haftarah for the Torah portion Shelach, the story of the earlier spies, and the Talmud remembers Rahab as a convert who joined the people of Israel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, be strong, three times to Joshua and once back from the people. Your line was be strong, again. Today, two spies, and the woman who saves them.

Night, in Jericho. A knock at a door in the city wall: the king's men. Two strangers were seen coming into this house, they say. Bring them out. Upstairs, on the flat roof, two men lie very still under stalks of flax laid out to dry. The woman of the house is called Rahab. What she says in the next minute decides whether those men live. She's not from their people. She owes them nothing. And she's about to bet her own family on them.
screen: `A KNOCK IN THE CITY WALL.` → `TWO SPIES UNDER THE FLAX.` → `RAHAB DECIDES.`

segments.voice: She tells the soldiers: yes, men came, but they left at dusk, before the gate closed. Go after them quickly and you'll catch them. The soldiers run off toward the river. Then she climbs to the roof, and she talks. We've heard what your God did, she says, how the sea dried up in front of you. Our hearts melted. And then, from a stranger, a sentence of faith: the Lord your God is God in heaven above and on the earth below. Then she bargains. I was kind to you; swear to be kind to my father's house: my father and mother, my brothers and sisters, and everyone who belongs to them. The spies swear. Her house is built into the wall itself, so she lets them down by a rope through her window. They leave her a sign: tie "this line of scarlet thread" in that window, gather your family inside, and whoever is in the house will be safe. The Hebrew calls her a zonah, a harlot. The ancient Aramaic translation, and Rashi after it, read the word as an innkeeper, a woman who sold food; other readers keep the plain sense. Either way, she lives at the edge of the city, and she's the one who sees clearly. The Talmud remembers that she converted and joined Israel, and tells that prophets came from her line. And the Hebrew word for that red cord is tikvah, the same word Hebrew uses for hope.

700.title: Twelve stones (Joshua 3–4)
700.hook: the priests step into the Jordan first, and twelve stones are set up so children will ask "What mean ye by these stones?"
700.howItsDone: At the Passover seder the story is told in answer to children's questions, and some families keep objects at home that prompt a story to be retold.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rahab, the woman on the wall, and her scarlet cord. Your line was the scarlet cord. Today, the people cross the river.

The river is in flood. The book stops to tell us that: at harvest time the Jordan runs over all its banks. On the near side stands a whole people, with children, animals, everything they own. Nobody builds a bridge. Nobody waits for the water to drop. The priests carrying the ark of the covenant walk to the edge first, and step in. The moment their feet touch the water, the river upstream stops and stands up in a heap, and the people cross on dry ground. And before anyone moves on, Joshua asks for stones.
screen: `THE JORDAN IN FLOOD.` → `THE PRIESTS STEP IN FIRST.` → `THE RIVER STOPS.`

segments.voice: Twelve men are chosen, one from each tribe. Each goes back into the riverbed, to the spot where the priests are standing, picks up a stone, and carries it out on his shoulder. Joshua sets the twelve up at Gilgal, where they camp that night. Why? The answer is a question. These stones are a sign, so that when your children ask in time to come, "What mean ye by these stones?" you can tell them: the waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark. The memorial is built to be asked about. A pile of river stones doesn't explain itself. Someone has to say, I'll tell you. If that sounds familiar, it should. The Torah does the same at Passover: when your children say to you, "What mean ye by this service?" From Egypt to the Jordan, remembering runs through a child's question and a parent's story. The Hebrew behind in time to come is machar, the everyday word for tomorrow. The book expects the question soon, from the next generation. And there's a second pile. Joshua also sets up twelve stones in the middle of the Jordan, right where the priests' feet stood, and the text says they're there to this day. One pile on the bank, for everyone to see and ask about. One in the river, where the crossing happened.
screen: `ONE STONE FOR EACH TRIBE.` · `BUILT TO BE ASKED ABOUT.` · `MACHAR: TOMORROW.` · then, large: `WHAT MEAN YE BY THESE STONES?` · then: `A SECOND PILE, UNDER THE WATER.`

segments.voice: If there's a small stone nearby, a pebble from a plant pot, pick it up; if not, any small object within reach will do. Hold it in your palm, feel its weight, and give it one crossing from your life, a time something gave way when you didn't expect it to. Don't tell yourself the whole story; just name it, and let the stone hold it.
